read.sections.0.heading.source: New machines have changed work before
read.sections.0.heading.back: New machines have changed work before

read.sections.0.text.source: AI is not the first technology to change people's work. In England in the early 1800s, new machines in cloth factories began to do work that skilled cloth workers had done by hand. Between 1811 and 1816, some of these workers, known as Luddites, broke machines in protest, because the machines were taking their work. Much later, from the 1970s, cash machines slowly spread to banks in the United States. Many people expected bank tellers, who handle money at the counter, to disappear. Instead, a study from 2015 found that the number of tellers stayed about the same and even grew a little. Each branch needed fewer tellers, so banks could open more branches. Tellers spent less time counting cash and more time helping customers. That was one machine in one country, so it can't tell us what AI will do.
read.sections.0.text.back: AI is not the first technology that changed people's work. In England in the early 1800s, new machines in cloth factories began to do the work that skilled cloth workers used to do by hand. Between 1811 and 1816, some of these workers, known as the Luddites, broke machines as a form of protest, because the machines were taking their work. Long after that, from the 1970s, ATMs slowly spread to banks in the United States. Many people thought bank tellers, the staff who handle money at the counter, would disappear. In fact, a study from 2015 found that the number of tellers stayed more or less the same, and even grew a little. Each branch needed fewer tellers, so banks could open more branches. Tellers counted cash less and helped customers more. That was only one machine in one country, so that example can't tell us what AI will do.
read.sections.0.text.note: "Cash machines" is "mesin ATM", the everyday word; "teller bank" is common in Indonesia and explained in the same sentence. "Luddites" is "kaum Luddite" (the Luddites as a group); the checker may warn that the English plural does not appear.

read.sections.0.simpler.source: AI is not the first technology to change work. In the 1800s, new machines in England did the work of skilled cloth workers. Some workers, called Luddites, broke machines in protest. From the 1970s, banks in the United States got cash machines. Many thought bank workers at the counter would disappear. But a 2015 study found there were still about as many. Banks opened more branches. The workers counted less cash and helped customers more. That was one machine in one country. It can't tell us what AI will do.
read.sections.0.simpler.back: AI is not the first technology that changed work. In the 1800s, new machines in England did the work of skilled cloth workers. Some workers, called the Luddites, broke machines in protest. From the 1970s, banks in the United States had ATMs. Many people thought bank staff at the counter would disappear. But a 2015 study found their number stayed about the same. Banks opened more branches. The staff counted money less and helped customers more. That was only one machine in one country. That example can't tell us what AI will do.

read.sections.1.heading.back: AI changes the tasks inside jobs

read.sections.1.text.source: Most jobs are made of many tasks. A new technology may automate some tasks, but not the whole job. When spreadsheets came to office computers in the United States, many bookkeepers lost their work, but the number of accountants grew. In 2025, the ILO, the United Nations agency for work, studied AI tools that write and make things. Its researchers scored about 30,000 tasks for how much of each one these tools could do. They found that about one in four of the world's jobs has some exposure to these tools. Office jobs, such as clerks who type in data, have the most. Exposure tells us what the tools could do. It is not a count of jobs lost. The ILO says most of these jobs are more likely to change than to disappear, because people are still needed for many tasks.
read.sections.1.text.back: Most jobs are made of many tasks. A new technology can automate some tasks, but not the whole job. When spreadsheets began to be used on office computers in the United States, many bookkeepers lost their jobs, but the number of accountants actually grew. In 2025, the ILO, the UN body that deals with work, studied AI tools that can write and make things. Its researchers scored about 30,000 tasks: how much of each task these tools could do. They found that about one in four jobs in the world is exposed to some degree to these tools. Office jobs, such as administrative staff who type in data, are the most exposed. Exposure tells us what those tools could do. It is not a count of jobs lost. According to the ILO, most of these jobs are more likely to change than to disappear, because people are still needed for many tasks.
read.sections.1.text.note: "Has some exposure to" is "sedikit banyak terpapar" (is exposed to some degree), as before. "Clerks who type in data" is "petugas administrasi yang mengetik data".

read.sections.1.simpler.source: A job is made of many tasks. A new technology may automate some tasks, not the whole job. Spreadsheets did sums for office workers. Some people who added up numbers lost their work. But there were more accountants. In 2025, a United Nations group for work studied AI that writes and makes things. It checked about 30,000 tasks. About one in four jobs has some exposure to these tools. That means the tools could do some of the tasks. Office jobs have the most. This is not a count of lost jobs. Most of these jobs will likely change, not disappear.
read.sections.1.simpler.back: One job is made of many tasks. A new technology can automate some tasks, not the whole job. Spreadsheets did sums for office workers. Some people whose task was adding up numbers lost their jobs. But the number of accountants grew. In 2025, a UN body for work studied AI that can write and make things. It checked about 30,000 tasks. About one in four jobs is exposed to some degree to these tools. That means the tools could do some of their tasks. Office jobs are the most exposed. This is not a count of lost jobs. Most of these jobs will probably change, not disappear.

read.sections.2.text.source: The same change can affect people very differently. The ILO found that exposure is higher in richer countries: about one in three jobs, against about one in ten in the poorest countries. In richer countries, more of women's jobs than men's are in the most exposed group. Change can be uneven inside one office too. In the made-up town of Millbrook, the water office now works faster. After training, two clerks moved to the help desk, but the third lost her work. The ILO says talks between workers, employers and governments can help to manage these changes. Who gains depends partly on the choices people make.
read.sections.2.text.back: The same change can affect different people very differently. The ILO found that exposure is higher in richer countries: about one in three jobs, compared with about one in ten in the poorest countries. In richer countries, more of women's jobs than men's jobs are in the most exposed group. Change can also be uneven inside one office. In the made-up town of Millbrook, the water office now works faster. After training, two administrative staff moved to the help counter, but the third lost her job. According to the ILO, talks between workers, employers and governments can help to manage these changes. Who gains depends partly on the choices people make.
read.sections.2.text.note: "Employers" is "pemberi kerja", the word used in Indonesian labour law; "talks between workers, employers and governments" (social dialogue) is "pembicaraan antara pekerja, pemberi kerja dan pemerintah".

read.sections.2.simpler.source: Change can affect people in different ways. The ILO found more exposure in richer countries. There, about one in three jobs has some. In the poorest countries, it is about one in ten. In richer countries, more women's jobs than men's are very exposed. In made-up Millbrook, the water office works faster now. After training, two clerks moved to the help desk. The third clerk lost her work. Workers, employers and leaders can plan these changes together, the ILO says.
read.sections.2.simpler.back: Change can affect each person differently. The ILO found exposure is higher in richer countries. There, about one in three jobs is exposed. In the poorest countries, about one in ten. In richer countries, more women's jobs than men's are very exposed. In made-up Millbrook, the water office now works faster. After training, two staff moved to the help counter. The third staff member lost her job. Workers, employers and leaders can plan these changes together, the ILO says.

write.prompt.source: Choose one Millbrook worker. Explain which of their tasks changed, and who gained or lost. Then say how it is like or unlike one change from history in the lesson.
write.prompt.back: Choose one worker in Millbrook. Explain which task changed, and who gained or lost. Then say how that change is like or unlike one change from history in this lesson.

write.example.source: I chose the clerks at the Millbrook water office. The task that changed was typing up forms, because an AI tool now reads most of them. The office gained, because the work is faster. Ines gained too, because after training she moved to the help desk. The third clerk lost her work. This is like the bank tellers, because Ines's work moved towards helping people. It is also unlike them, because one clerk lost her job, while the number of tellers did not fall.
write.example.back: I chose the administrative staff at the Millbrook water office. The task that changed is typing forms, because now an AI tool reads most of those forms. The office gained, because the work became faster. Ines gained too, because after training she moved to the help counter. The third staff member lost her job. This is like the bank tellers, because Ines's work shifted to helping people. It is also unlike them, because one staff member lost her job, while the number of tellers did not go down.

watch.why.source: It looks back at a hundred years of worry about machines taking jobs, and asks who gains from new technology.

watch.beforeQuestion.source: Do you think new machines make more jobs or fewer jobs? Why?
watch.beforeQuestion.back: Do you think new machines make jobs more or fewer? Why?

watch.afterQuestion.source: Why does the video say that who gains from technology depends on people's choices?
watch.afterQuestion.back: Why does the video say that who gains from technology depends on human choices?

watch.summary.source: This video asks if machines and AI will take away people's jobs. People have worried about this many times before. In the United States, machines replaced many workers in the 1920s and 1930s. It happened again around 1960. Machines took work on farms, in factories and on telephone lines. But most people still found work. Technology makes some new jobs, such as building and fixing machines. It also makes things cheaper. Then people spend money on other things, like haircuts or eating out, and those need workers too. Some experts say AI is different, because it can do many kinds of work. The video says the bigger question may be who gains. The gains from technology have not been shared fairly. The rules people choose can change that.
watch.summary.back: This video asks whether machines and AI will take people's jobs. People have often worried about this before. In the United States, machines replaced many workers in the 1920s and 1930s. It happened again around 1960. Machines took work in farming, in factories and in telephone networks. But most people still got work. Technology creates some new jobs, like making and fixing machines. Technology also makes goods cheaper. Then people spend their money on other things, like haircuts or eating out, and all of those need workers too. Some experts say AI is different, because AI can do many kinds of work. The video says the bigger question may be who gains. The gains from technology have not been shared fairly. The rules humans choose can change that.

sensitiveNotes.1.source: Britannica notes that the government punished the Luddites harshly, including hangings. The lesson leaves this out; if learners ask, keep it short and factual.

educatorNotes.0.source: One estimate in learner text, on purpose: the ILO's Generative AI and jobs, a 2025 update (Gmyrek and others, 20 May 2025, with Poland's NASK; ILO Working Paper 140). It scored nearly 30,000 tasks for how far generative AI could do them. 25% of the world's jobs are in occupations with some exposure (34% in high-income countries, 11% in low-income ones); 3.3% are in the most exposed group, mostly clerical jobs such as data entry clerks and typists; in high-income countries that group is 9.6% of women's jobs and 3.5% of men's. The ILO says the figures reflect potential exposure, an upper limit, not the actual effect on employment; it expects most jobs to be transformed rather than made redundant, though efficiency gains could still reduce demand for workers. Other estimates, such as the IMF's (January 2024: almost 40% of jobs exposed to AI in general), cover a wider set of technologies and use another method, so they can't be set beside the ILO's number; the lesson uses only the ILO's. The bank teller example is US data from the 1970s to the 2000s (James Bessen, 2015), and the spreadsheet example is from NPR (2015); each is one past case, not a forecast for AI.
educatorNotes.0.back: Learner text deliberately has only one estimate: the ILO's Generative AI and jobs, a 2025 update (Gmyrek and colleagues, 20 May 2025, with Poland's NASK; ILO Working Paper 140). It scored nearly 30,000 tasks for how far generative AI could do them. 25% of the world's jobs are in occupations exposed to some degree (34% in high-income countries, 11% in low-income countries); 3.3% are in the most exposed group, mostly administrative jobs such as data entry staff and typists; in high-income countries that group covers 9.6% of women's jobs and 3.5% of men's. The ILO says the figures show possible exposure, an upper limit, not the real effect on employment; it expects most jobs to change rather than become unneeded, although efficiency gains could still reduce the need for workers. Other estimates, such as the IMF's (January 2024: almost 40% of jobs exposed to AI in general), cover wider technology and use another method, so they can't be set beside the ILO's figure; this lesson uses only the ILO's. The bank teller example is US data from the 1970s to the 2000s (James Bessen, 2015), and the spreadsheet example is from NPR (2015); each is one past case, not a forecast about AI.

educatorNotes.1.source: The Speak discussion has no single right answer. Ideas might include retraining the clerk for another task, moving more slowly, or sharing the remaining work; ask who would have to agree (the employer, the workers, a union or the government), which links to the ILO's point about talks between them. A teacher could add a local example of a tool that changed work, without asking about anyone's own job.
educatorNotes.1.back: The discussion in the Speak step has no single right answer. Ideas could be retraining that staff member for another task, making the change more slowly, or sharing the remaining work; ask who would have to agree to it (the employer, the workers, a trade union or the government), which links to the ILO's point about talks between them. A teacher can add a local example of a tool that changed work, without asking about anyone's job.
